We need to differentiate among Al3+, Cd2+, Mg2+, Pb2+, Zn2+, Hg2+, Hg2+2 (mercury(I) dimer). Typical tests:

- Add NaOH (or KOH) to get precipitates: Al(OH)3 white gelatinous, Mg(OH)2 white precipitate that dissolves in excess, Zn(OH)2 white precipitate that dissolves in excess, Cd(OH)2 white precipitate that dissolves in excess, Pb(OH)2 white precipitate that is insoluble in excess? Actually Pb(OH)2 is slightly soluble in excess OH? Not sure. Hg2+ (Hg2+2) forms Hg2Cl2 white precipitate with Cl-, but we already did chloride test? Not sure.

- Add ammonium hydroxide: Al(OH)3 precipitate, Zn(OH)2 precipitate dissolves in excess NH3 forming [Zn(NH3)4]2+, Cd(OH)2 also dissolves? Cd forms [Cd(NH3)4]2+? I think Cd also dissolves in excess NH3. Mg(OH)2 does not dissolve in NH3. Pb(OH)2 dissolves? Not sure.

- Add H2S in acidic solution: CdS black precipitate, PbS black, ZnS white? Actually ZnS is white precipitate in acidic H2S? ZnS is white, but in acidic solution it's not precipitated? ZnS precipitates in alkaline H2S. So we can use H2S acidic to precipitate CdS (black) and PbS (black). Al and Mg no sulfide precipitate.

- Add Na2CO3: MgCO3 white precipitate, CaCO3 white, but Al forms Al2(CO3)3 which hydrolyzes? Not sure.

- Add K2CrO4: PbCrO4 yellow precipitate, CdCrO4? Not typical. ZnCrO4? Not typical. Al no.

Thus a good test: add K2CrO4 to see yellow precipitate indicates Pb2+. Also add H2S acidic to see black precipitate for Cd2+ or Pb2+. Distinguish.

Also test with NaOH: Mg(OH)2 precipitate that is white and insoluble in excess; Al(OH)3 precipitate that is gelatinous and dissolves in excess NaOH? Actually Al(OH)3 is amphoteric, dissolves in excess NaOH forming [Al(OH)4]-. Zn(OH)2 also amphoteric dissolves in excess NaOH. Cd(OH)2 also amphoteric? I think Cd(OH)2 is slightly amphoteric but dissolves in strong base. Pb(OH)2 is not amphoteric (insoluble in excess). Hg2+ forms Hg2(OH)2? Not typical.

Thus we can perform a test: add K2CrO4 to sample.
